newsitem.title: USA: More Mississippi locks to reopen if water drops.
newsitem.headline: More Mississippi locks to reopen if water drops.

text.p: More locks along the upper Mississippi River are set to reopen by the end of the weekend if high waters continue to drop, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

Locks remained shut by high water from Lock and Dam 12 at Bellevue, Iowa, through Lock and Dam 17 at New Boston, Illinois. "These locks will reopen by the end of the weekend depending on how fast the water drops," said Bob Hildebrand, Chief Warrant Officer, U.S. Coast Guard, Marine Safety Office, at St Louis.
Lock and Dam 11 near Dubuque, Iowa, opened to navigation on Tuesday, but with certain restrictions.
River officials said the high water on the Mississippi resulted from snow melt after above-average snow hit Wisconsin, Minnesota and the Dakotas last winter.
"It was mostly the snow melt in Minnesota and Wisconsin that contributed to the high water levels. There has been rain this spring but that was not a main factor," Hildebrand said.
Mariners should proceed slowly from Minneapolis to Guttenberg, Iowa, to prevent wake damage to levees and property along the river banks, he said.
"The same thing holds from Clinton, Iowa, to Davenport, Iowa," Hildebrand said.
In addition, the safety zone remained in effect for a 10-mile stretch in St Louis harbor, the Coast Guard said.
The Mississippi River at St Louis was at 30.2 feet, right at flood stage. "It is cresting now, but until the water level gets below 25 feet the safety zone stays in effect," Hildebrand said.
As of Tuesday, 30 southbound tows and 57 northbound tows between Minneapolis-St Paul and St Louis could not move, which was considered light traffic, Hildebrand said.
At Davenport, Iowa, water levels stood at 19 feet, above the 15-feet flood stage.

"It is cresting right now," Hildebrand said. "Now the water is slowing dropping from St Paul all the way down to Keokuk, Iowa, and the rest of the river is moderating a little bit. It is like a real flat wave that is just bouncing up and down the Mississippi River."
